stem: A JUnit Jupiter test class has no `@TestInstance` annotation and declares three test methods, one of them disabled with `@Disabled`. How many instances of the class does JUnit create?
key: Three, including one for the disabled method
distractors: One, shared by all three test methods
One for the whole test run, shared with other test classes
Two, because no instance is created for the disabled method
explanation: The test class is still instantiated when a test method is disabled via a condition, so three instances are created. One instance shared by all three methods is wrong because the per-method lifecycle is the default behavior in JUnit Jupiter, and so is one instance for the whole test run. Two instances are wrong because a method disabled via a condition does not stop the class from being instantiated for it.
extract: the test class will still be instantiated if a given test method is disabled via a condition

stem: A JUnit Jupiter test passes a `Supplier<String>` as the failure message of an assertion, for example `() -> buildReport()`. Which statement about that message is correct?
key: It is evaluated only when the assertion fails
distractors: It is evaluated before the assertion runs, on every call
It is evaluated once, when the test class is instantiated
It is rejected, because the message parameter must be a `String`
explanation: A message given as a `Supplier<String>` is only evaluated when the assertion fails. Evaluating it before the assertion on every call is wrong because the message is evaluated lazily, and so is evaluating it once at instantiation. Rejecting it is wrong because the message can be either a `String` or a `Supplier<String>`.
extract: it is only evaluated when the assertion fails

stem: A test calls a Spring-managed bean from inside `assertTimeoutPreemptively` while Spring's test-managed transaction is active. What happens to the bean's database changes after the test finishes?
key: They are committed, even though the test-managed transaction is rolled back
distractors: They are rolled back together with the test-managed transaction
They are rolled back, because the executable runs in the thread of the calling code
They are rolled back, because Spring binds transaction state to the whole JVM
explanation: The bean's actions are committed to the persistent store even though the test-managed transaction is rolled back. A rollback together with the test-managed transaction is wrong because those actions will not be rolled back with it. A rollback in the calling thread is wrong because `assertTimeoutPreemptively` runs the executable in a different thread. A rollback through JVM-wide transaction state is wrong because Spring binds transaction state to the current thread through a `ThreadLocal`.
extract: such actions will be committed to the persistent store (e.g., relational database) even though the test-managed transaction is rolled back

stem: A Mockito test stubs `when(list.get(0)).thenReturn("a")` and, later in the same test, `when(list.get(0)).thenReturn("b")`. What does `list.get(0)` return afterwards?
distractors: `"a"`, because the first stubbing is kept
`null`, because the second stubbing resets the mock
An exception, because the same call was stubbed twice
explanation: When the same method is stubbed with the same arguments many times, the last stubbing is more important, so `"b"` is returned. Keeping the first stubbing is wrong for the same reason: the last one wins. Returning `null` is wrong because once stubbed, the method will always return a stubbed value. An exception is wrong because stubbing can be overridden.
extract: Last stubbing is more important - when you stubbed the same method with

stem: A JUnit 5 test class uses the Testcontainers extension and must share one container between all its test methods. How is the `@Container` field declared?
key: As a static field in a top level test class
distractors: As a non-static field in a top level test class
As a non-static field in a `@Nested` test class
As a static field in a `@Nested` test class
explanation: Shared containers are defined as static fields in a top level test class and annotated with `@Container`. A non-static field in a top level class is wrong because a shared container must be a static field. A non-static field in a `@Nested` class is wrong because shared containers can't be declared inside nested test classes. A static field in a `@Nested` class is wrong because nested test classes are non-static and therefore can't have static fields.
extract: Shared containers are defined as static fields in a top level test class and have to be annotated with @Container.

stem: The snippet builds fixed clocks for the instant `2026-03-31T23:30:00Z` in `UTC` and `Europe/Madrid`, then checks an invoice due on `2026-03-31` against each clock. What does it print?
distractors:
2026-03-31
2026-03-31
false
false
true

2026-03-31
2026-04-01
false
true
false
explanation: The same instant is `2026-03-31` in `UTC` and `2026-04-01` in `Europe/Madrid`, so only the second clock finds the invoice overdue, and both clocks hold equal instants. The output with equal dates is wrong because the zone converts the instant to a different date. The output with `false` for the last line is wrong because the zone does not change the instant. The output with `true` for `UTC` is wrong because `isAfter` is false for a date equal to the due date.

stem: The snippet checks `isExpired` with a fixed clock one second before, exactly at and one second after the expiry, then reads the clock twice. What does it print?
key:
offset -1: false
offset 0: false
offset 1: true
same instant twice: true
distractors:
offset -1: false
offset 0: true
offset 1: true
same instant twice: true

offset -1: false
offset 0: false
offset 1: true
same instant twice: false

offset -1: true
offset 0: false
offset 1: false
same instant twice: true
explanation: `isAfter` is false at the expiry and true one second later, and a fixed clock returns an equal instant each time. The output with `true` at the expiry is wrong because `isAfter` excludes an equal instant. The output ending in `false` is wrong because a fixed clock does not tick. The output starting with `true` is wrong because one second before the expiry the instant is not after it.

stem: The snippet runs `midpoint` as `(low + high) / 2` on three input pairs, the last one near `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, and prints the expected value computed with `long`. What does it print?
explanation: The sum of the last pair overflows `int` to `-3`, and `-3 / 2` truncates to `-1`, while the `long` computation gives `2147483646`. The output without a difference is wrong because `int` addition overflows silently. The output with `-2` is wrong because integer division truncates toward zero. The output with `expected -1` is wrong because the expected value is computed with `long`.

stem: In the Mockito Javadoc example, `get(0)` on a mocked `LinkedList` is stubbed with `thenReturn("first")`. What does the Javadoc say about also calling `verify(mockedList).get(0)`?
distractors: Impossible, because a stubbed call is not recorded as an interaction
Required, because a wrong return value would otherwise go unnoticed
Required, because `verify` works only on calls that were stubbed first
explanation: Verifying a stubbed invocation is possible but usually redundant. Calling it impossible is wrong because a mock remembers all interactions. Calling it required to notice a wrong return value is wrong because if the code cares what `get(0)` returns, something else breaks, often before `verify()` is executed. Calling it required for `verify` to work is wrong because code that does not care what `get(0)` returns should not stub it.
extract: Although it is possible to verify a stubbed invocation, usually it's just redundant

stem: A JUnit Jupiter test method is annotated with `@ParameterizedTest` to run once per argument. What does the user guide require the test to declare for that to work?
key: At least one source that provides the arguments for each invocation
distractors: A `@Test` annotation next to `@ParameterizedTest`, which marks the method as a test
A single argument source, because the method runs exactly once with all the arguments
A reporting rule that merges all invocations into one test result
explanation: The test must declare at least one source that provides the arguments for each invocation. Keeping `@Test` next to `@ParameterizedTest` is ruled out because a parameterized test uses the `@ParameterizedTest` annotation instead of `@Test`. A single run with all the arguments is ruled out because a parameterized test runs a test method multiple times with different arguments. Merging the invocations into one result is ruled out because each invocation is reported separately.

stem: A JUnit Jupiter test class is annotated with `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)`. Which statement about its test instances is correct according to the user guide?
key: All test methods execute on the same test instance
distractors: JUnit creates a new instance of the class before each test method, as in the default mode
State in instance variables never needs resetting, because each method gets a fresh instance
`@BeforeAll` and `@AfterAll` must still be declared on static methods
explanation: All test methods execute on the same test instance, and a new instance is created once per test class. A new instance before each method is ruled out because that per-method lifecycle is the default, and `PER_CLASS` is the annotation chosen to run all methods on the same instance. Never resetting instance state is ruled out because tests that rely on state stored in instance variables may need to reset it in `@BeforeEach` or `@AfterEach`. Static-only lifecycle methods are ruled out because the per-class mode makes it possible to declare `@BeforeAll` and `@AfterAll` on non-static methods.

stem: A test builds a clock with `Clock.fixed(instant, zone)` from `java.time`. Which statement about that clock is correct according to its Javadoc?
key: The clock is immutable, thread-safe and `Serializable`
distractors: The clock starts at the given instant and then advances with the system clock
The clock is mutable, so a test can move it to another instant after creation
The zone shifts the instant that the clock returns by the offset of the zone
explanation: The returned implementation is immutable, thread-safe and `Serializable`. A clock that advances from the given instant is ruled out because the fixed clock always returns the same instant. A mutable clock is ruled out because the returned implementation is immutable. A zone that shifts the returned instant is ruled out because the zone is only used to convert the instant to date-time.

stem: A Mockito mock of a class is created and none of its methods is stubbed. According to the Javadoc, what does a call to an unstubbed method that returns an `int` give?
distractors: `Integer.MIN_VALUE`
explanation: An unstubbed method that returns an `int` gives `0`, the default the Javadoc names for an `int` or `Integer`. The numbers `1`, `-1` and `Integer.MIN_VALUE` fail because the Javadoc names `0` as that default.
